Medical History

- Current health issues and chronic disease risk factors (e.g., hypertension, diabetes):  Acute wheeze and exertional shortness of breath x 2–3 days; history of asthma (childhood “quite bad,” intermittent adult symptoms); atopy (hay fever, eczema).  
- Family history of chronic conditions (e.g., CVD, diabetes):  Not recorded.  
- Current medications including OTC and traditional medicines:  Salbutamol inhaler (short-acting beta-agonist) PRN; dose/route/frequency not documented. Regular antihistamine recommended OTC; agent/dose not documented.

- Sexual/reproductive health status and risks:  Not recorded.

Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)

- Summary: Adult with history of significant childhood asthma and atopy presents with 2–3 days of wheeze, exertional dyspnea (unable to walk to work), dry cough, and occasional difficulty completing sentences during the flare. No chest pain, no hemoptysis, no nocturnal awakenings. Afebrile by measurement (37°C). Non-smoker.  
- Working diagnosis: Asthma exacerbation, likely triggered by viral upper respiratory infection and/or seasonal allergens.  
- Supporting DDx (consistent with transcript):  
  - Viral URI/acute bronchitis with bronchospasm (possible trigger).  
  - COVID-19 infection precipitating asthma symptoms (less likely given afebrile measurement and no classic features reported).  
- Considerations (lower likelihood): Community-acquired pneumonia (no fever/sputum), pulmonary embolism (no pleuritic chest pain, hemoptysis, risk factors).  
- Management plan per consultation:  
  - Increase salbutamol use initially: 2–4 puffs every 4 hours (dose schedule advised; exact device/dose not documented).  
  - Prescribe spacer for inhaler technique; pharmacist to demonstrate use.  
  - Prescribe peak flow meter; patient to record morning and evening values daily for a week.  
  - Start regular antihistamine (OTC) for allergic symptoms; specific agent/dose not documented.  
  - Safety net: Call back urgently if fever develops or wheeze/shortness of breath worsens.  
  - Arrange review in ~1 week to assess symptoms and peak flow diary; may consider additional controller medication at review.  

Health Promotion & Planning

- Education on chronic disease prevention and lifestyle modification:  Inhaler technique with spacer; regular monitoring using peak flow; recognition of worsening symptoms; trigger awareness (allergens/viral illness).  
- Patient health goals and priorities:  Not recorded.  
- Eligibility for GP Management Plan (GPMP) or Team Care Arrangements (TCA):  Not recorded.  
- Referrals (allied health, Quitline, AOD services, Aboriginal health worker, or social supports):  Pharmacist for spacer technique and peak flow meter instruction.  
- Follow-up and recall appointments scheduled:  Review planned in 1 week; earlier if clinical deterioration.

- Social work or housing support referral if social determinants affect health:  Not recorded.  

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx)

- Asthma exacerbation (High): Acute wheeze and exertional dyspnea in a patient with known atopic asthma and intermittent SABA use.  
- Viral URI/acute bronchitis with bronchospasm (Medium): Short-duration dry cough and wheeze commonly trigger asthma flares.  
- COVID-19–related bronchospasm (Medium-Low): Cough/dyspnea could fit, but afebrile by measurement and no specific features reported.  

Quality checks

- Missing expected elements: Full vitals (BP, pulse, SpO2), BMI/anthropometrics, immunization review (influenza, COVID-19, pneumococcal, shingles, tetanus), chronic disease screening (diabetes, CVD risk, cancer screening), hearing/vision, mood screening, urinalysis, and baseline labs not recorded.  
- Internal conflicts/contradictions: Patient reported “fever” but measured temperature was 37°C (afebrile). Medication history conflict noted: patient initially stated stopping asthma medications 3–4 years ago, later reported using salbutamol every few weeks.  
- Transcript quality notes: Some answers unclear/indeterminate (timing of prior asthma episodes); telehealth format without physical exam or objective measures. Additionally, assessment template is for adults 55+, but patient’s stated DOB (1990) suggests younger age—mismatch with template (conflict noted).
